title: Pride of birth
hookLine: a proud young brahmin insults the Sakyans, and his own ancestry comes out
carry: no talk of birth at the summit

cards: A well-known brahmin teacher named Pokkharasati wants to know if the Buddha is really who people say. So he sends his student, Ambattha, a young man who has mastered the Vedas. Ambattha arrives and doesn't sit down.
He walks around while the Buddha sits, talking at him. And when the Buddha asks if that's how he speaks to elders, Ambattha starts on the Sakyans, the Buddha's own clan.
Once, he says, I went to their assembly hall in Kapilavatthu, and they laughed, and nobody offered me a seat. They're menials.

teach.h: A QUAIL CHIRPS IN ITS OWN NEST
teach.b: The Buddha's first reply is gentle. Even a little quail can chirp as it likes in its own nest; Kapilavatthu is the Sakyans' home. But Ambattha insults them again, and again.
So the Buddha asks a simple question: what's your clan? Kanhayana, says Ambattha. And the Buddha tells the old story.
The Sakyans trace their line to an ancient king, Okkaka. That king had a slave woman, and she had a son named Kanha. Ambattha's clan descends from him.
By the standards Ambattha himself has been using, his own ancestor was the son of a slave in the Sakyans' royal house. Ambattha won't answer at first.
The text says a spirit holding a thunderbolt appeared above him, and he finally admits: yes, that's what my teachers say. His fellow students start jeering. And here's the turn.
Don't look down on Ambattha, he says. That Kanha became a great sage, and a king gave him his own daughter in marriage. So the story doesn't end as a humiliation.
Read this way, it shows that pride of birth falls apart when you look closely. The Pali word is jati: birth. Then the teaching.

teach.h: NO TALK OF BIRTH AT THE SUMMIT
teach.b: In the highest knowledge and conduct, there's no talk of birth, no talk of clan, no talk of who is worthy of whom.

That talk belongs to marriages and family arrangements. Look back at the week: the moonlit ride, the dodging answers, honored, wings, the gem and thread, regret confessed. And now a family tree, shaken.

how: In Buddhist monastic communities, people from every background ordain together, and order is counted from ordination, not birth; the teaching that conduct, not lineage, makes a person noble is repeated across the discourses.

o: a vow made at a child's naming
birth, and the group one is born into
the wealth and land a family owns

games.q: pride of birth: tap the pairs.
p: the ancestor, son of a slave woman

s: the Buddha tells the story of Kanha to humiliate Ambattha
when the other students jeer, he stops them and says Kanha became a great sage.
the Buddha first answers with the image of a quail in its own nest
the Sakyans were at home in Kapilavatthu, free to act as they liked.
the discourse says birth matters in the highest knowledge and conduct
there's no talk of birth or clan there; that talk belongs to marriage arrangements.

games.q: Ambattha has finally admitted his clan's ancestry, and his fellow students are jeering at him. you're the Buddha. what do you do?
o: tell them not to look down on him, and praise his ancestor.
join in to drive the lesson home.
games.why: the Buddha defends him: Kanha became a great sage, and a king gave him his daughter. the point was the emptiness of pride, not Ambattha's shame.

practice: If a pride of family comes to mind, our people, our name, our side of town, our school, hold it gently and notice any small lift it gives.
Then picture the family tree going back past anyone you know, to people of every kind, and let the lift soften; you can keep loving your family and just set down the ranking.

wordCard.voice: Jati. Birth, also the group one is born into: it matters to marriages and family trees, and not at all to knowledge and good conduct.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit jati: birth, also the group one is born into. the ground of Ambattha's pride.

carryVoice: Your line: no talk of birth at the summit. What counts there is knowledge and conduct. Day five hundred thirty-two, done.
